subject: A Trip to the Moon
text: American labs pirated it so widely that its maker sent his brother to New York to stop them; he earned almost nothing from its success there.

subject: The Arrival of a Train at La Ciotat
text: Audiences were said to have screamed and run from the oncoming train. No contemporary report of the panic has ever been found.

subject: The Great Train Robbery
text: Its closing shot, a bandit firing straight at the audience, could be shown at the start or the end; projectionists chose.

subject: The Birth of a Nation
text: The first film shown at the White House. Its revival of the Klan's image helped refound the real Klan that year.

subject: Nosferatu
text: The widow of the novelist it copied sued and won; a court ordered every print destroyed. A few survived.

subject: Nosferatu
text: Legend has it {Max Schreck} really was a vampire, a story later turned into a film of its own.

subject: Battleship Potemkin
text: There was no massacre on the Odessa steps; the scene invented one so vividly that it is remembered as history.

subject: The General
text: The locomotive crashing through the burning bridge was real, and the single most expensive shot of the silent era. The wreck stayed in the riverbed for decades.

subject: Metropolis
text: A quarter of it was lost for eighty years until a battered print turned up in a Buenos Aires museum in 2008.

subject: The Jazz Singer
text: It is mostly silent; the famous synchronised talk was ad-libbed by its star between songs.

subject: Wings
text: Its director was a real First World War pilot, and its stars learned to fly for it.

subject: The Passion of Joan of Arc
text: The original negative burned, then so did the director's reassembled version. A complete print was found in 1981 in a Norwegian mental hospital's cupboard.

subject: Un Chien Andalou
text: At its premiere {Luis Buñuel} is said to have kept stones in his pockets to throw at the audience if they booed. They applauded.

subject: All Quiet on the Western Front
text: Nazi activists released mice and stink bombs at its Berlin screenings until it was banned.

subject: Frankenstein
text: The monster's flat head and bolts were a makeup man's invention; the studio copyrighted the look.

subject: M
text: The killer whistles a tune from a Grieg suite; its actor couldn't whistle, so the director whistled it himself.

subject: King Kong
text: Kong was an eighteen-inch model covered in rabbit fur; the fur rippling between frames is the animators' fingerprints.

subject: It Happened One Night
text: When its star took off his shirt to reveal no vest, undershirt sales were said to plunge.

subject: Modern Times
text: The tramp finally speaks: a song in a nonsense language, because he lost the lyrics written on his cuffs.

subject: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs
text: Hollywood called it the folly; it became the highest-grossing sound film yet made.

subject: La Grande Illusion
text: Goebbels named it cinematic enemy number one; the Germans seized the negative in Paris, and it was found after the war in Moscow.

subject: The Wizard of Oz
text: The original Tin Man was poisoned by the aluminium makeup dust and spent weeks in hospital; his replacement's makeup was a paste.

subject: The Wizard of Oz
text: A dark story says a crew member's suicide can be seen in the trees in one scene. It is a large bird from the studio zoo.

subject: Gone with the Wind
text: Its producer is said to have been fined five thousand dollars for the last line's swear word. In fact the censors had changed the rules weeks earlier to allow it.

subject: Stagecoach
text: Its director's favourite location, a Navajo valley on the Utah border, appeared here for the first time; he went back for decades.

subject: Citizen Kane
text: The newspaper magnate it portrayed banned any mention of it in his papers and tried to buy the negative to burn it.

subject: Citizen Kane
text: Rosebud was said to be the magnate's private nickname for part of his mistress's body. Its writer never confirmed it.

subject: Casablanca
text: The script was being written day by day; nobody, including its stars, knew which man she would leave with until the end.

subject: Casablanca
text: Nobody in it ever says "Play it again, Sam."

subject: Double Indemnity
text: The novelist's writing partner on the script was a mystery writer who loathed the director, and later called it the most agonising experience of his life.

subject: It's a Wonderful Life
text: The snow was a new formula of foamite, soap and water, invented because cornflakes crunched too loudly.

subject: It's a Wonderful Life
text: A flop on release, it became a Christmas staple only after a copyright lapse let television stations show it for free.

subject: Bicycle Thieves
text: Its lead was a factory worker who never found another good role and returned to the factory.

subject: The Third Man
text: The zither player was found playing in a Vienna beer garden; his theme topped the charts across the world.

subject: The Third Man
text: The cuckoo clock speech was written by its star, who borrowed the line from an old Hungarian play, he said, though the Swiss pointed out the clock is from Germany.

subject: Sunset Boulevard
text: Its silent star had really been directed by the actor who plays her butler; the film she watches is their abandoned picture.

subject: Rashomon
text: Its studio didn't understand it and didn't submit it to Venice; an Italian film scout did, and it won.

subject: Singin' in the Rain
text: Its star had a high fever when he danced the title number in the studio rain.

subject: Tokyo Story
text: Almost every shot is taken from the height of a person kneeling on a tatami mat.

subject: Seven Samurai
text: The final battle was shot in February in freezing rain and mud, with fire engines providing the downpour.

subject: Godzilla
text: The monster was a man in a suit weighing about a hundred kilos; its wearer could last only a few minutes before passing out.

subject: Rear Window
text: The whole courtyard was one set, the biggest ever built at the studio, with thirty-one apartments.

subject: On the Waterfront
text: The taxi-cab scene's backdrop was missing, so the director hung a Venetian blind over the back window.

subject: Pather Panchali
text: Shot on weekends over three years, with its director pawning his wife's jewellery; the state government finally paid to finish it, believing it was about road improvement.

subject: Rebel Without a Cause
text: It opened a month after its star was killed in his Porsche.

subject: The Searchers
text: A teenage fan named a band after its hero's catchphrase; it became a hit song that summer.

subject: The Seventh Seal
text: The famous dance of death on the hillside was shot in a hurry at the end of the day with crew members and passing tourists in the costumes.

subject: Vertigo
text: A flop on release, it later topped the most famous critics' poll as the greatest film ever made, ending the newspaper-tycoon picture's fifty-year reign.

subject: Ben-Hur
text: The chariot race took five weeks to film on an eighteen-acre set in Rome.

subject: Ben-Hur
text: A stuntman was said to have died in the chariot race and been left in the cut. He did not; the crash was a planned stunt and he survived.

subject: Some Like It Hot
text: Its star needed 47 takes to say "It's me, Sugar."

subject: Psycho
text: Its director bought up as many copies of the novel as he could so nobody would know the ending, and audiences were not admitted after the start.

subject: Psycho
text: The shower scene's blood is chocolate syrup; the stabbing sound is a knife going into a casaba melon.

subject: La Dolce Vita
text: A photographer character's name, Paparazzo, gave the world its word for celebrity photographers.

subject: Breakfast at Tiffany's
text: The novelist wanted a different blonde star for the lead and felt betrayed when the studio cast the dark-haired one.

subject: Lawrence of Arabia
text: The match cut from a blown-out match to a desert sunrise was meant as a dissolve; the editor tried the straight cut and it stayed.

subject: Dr. No
text: The series' famous gun-barrel opening was designed by a title artist in an afternoon; the stuntman in it is not the star.

subject: 8½
text: Its director taped a note to the camera reminding himself it was a comedy.

subject: Dr. Strangelove
text: The war room's table was covered in green baize, like a poker table, though the film is black and white.

subject: Dr. Strangelove
text: A custard-pie fight originally ended the film. It was cut after a preview; it was too much fun, the director decided.

subject: The Sound of Music
text: The real family left Austria by train, not over the mountains; the film's mountain would have led them into Germany.

subject: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly
text: The Spanish army built the bridge for the film; the crew blew it up before the cameras were rolling, and it had to be rebuilt.

subject: Blowup
text: The park in the film was painted greener for the shoot, grass and all.

subject: The Graduate
text: The woman playing the seducing mother was only six years older than the actor playing the student.

subject: Bonnie and Clyde
text: Its studio head hated it and buried it; a critic's rave and its star's lobbying got it a second release, and it became a smash.

subject: 2001: A Space Odyssey
text: The apes' eyes glow in the dawn scenes because the African backgrounds were front-projected and the reflective screen lit up their pupils.

subject: 2001: A Space Odyssey
text: The computer's name is said to be the computer company's initials shifted back one letter. Its writer always denied it was deliberate.

subject: Rosemary's Baby
text: The building it was shot in became famous as the home where a Beatle was killed outside twelve years later.

subject: Midnight Cowboy
text: I'm walkin' here! was improvised when a real New York cab nearly ran the actors down during a hidden-camera take.

subject: Easy Rider
text: The campfire scene was played genuinely stoned, according to the cast.

subject: The Godfather
text: The horse's head was real, from a dog-food factory.

subject: The Godfather
text: The studio nearly fired its director several times in the first weeks; he is said to have kept a list of who was plotting against him.

subject: The Godfather
text: The studio wanted an actor almost anyone else for the lead; the screen test where he stuffed his cheeks with cotton wool won them round.

subject: The Exorcist
text: The shoot was called cursed: the set burned down and several people connected with it died within the year.

subject: Jaws
text: The mechanical shark kept sinking in salt water, so the director had to suggest it with music and floating barrels, which made the film.

subject: Jaws
text: The crew named the shark Bruce, after the director's lawyer.

subject: One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest
text: It was shot in a real Oregon state hospital, and many of the extras were patients.

subject: Taxi Driver
text: You talkin' to me? was improvised; the script just said the driver talks to himself in the mirror.

subject: Rocky
text: Its writer refused to sell the script unless he played the lead himself, though he had almost no money.

subject: Star Wars
text: Almost everyone expected it to flop, including its director, who went to Hawaii on opening weekend to avoid the reviews.

subject: Star Wars
text: The robot pair were based on the bickering peasants of a Japanese samurai film.

subject: Annie Hall
text: It was going to be a murder mystery called Anhedonia; the mystery was cut in editing and became a different film years later.

subject: Close Encounters of the Third Kind
text: The five-note motif was chosen from more than three hundred combinations.

subject: Alien
text: The cast did not know exactly what would burst out of the chest; their shock as the blood hit them was real.

subject: Apocalypse Now
text: A typhoon destroyed the sets, its star had a heart attack, and the shoot ran from sixteen weeks to more than two hundred days.

subject: Apocalypse Now
text: Its director is said to have threatened suicide during the shoot and to have told the Côte festival that his film was not about Vietnam, it was Vietnam.

subject: The Shining
text: The "Here's Johnny" line was improvised; the director, who hadn't watched American late-night television, almost cut it.

subject: The Shining
text: The pages of the writer's endless manuscript were really typed, hundreds of them, and retyped in other languages for the dubbed versions.

subject: Raging Bull
text: Its star gained some thirty kilos to play the fighter in old age, shutting the production down for months to eat.

subject: Raiders of the Lost Ark
text: The hero shoots the swordsman because his actor had dysentery and couldn't face the planned fight.

subject: E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial
text: A chocolate maker turned down having its sweets in it; the rival brand's sales jumped by two-thirds.

subject: Blade Runner
text: Tears in rain was rewritten by its actor the night before the scene.

subject: Fitzcarraldo
text: The steamship really was hauled over a hill; no models were used.

subject: Scarface
text: Its lead burned his hand on a gun barrel and spent two weeks unable to work.

subject: The Terminator
text: Its director sold the rights for one dollar on condition he got to direct.

subject: Back to the Future
text: Its original lead was replaced after five weeks of shooting; the new one was filming a sitcom by day and the film by night.

subject: Ran
text: The castle burned in the film was built on the slopes of Mount Fuji and burned for real, in one take.

subject: Aliens
text: The crew in England had never heard of its director's earlier film and didn't take him seriously until it was screened for them.

subject: Top Gun
text: Navy recruitment booths were set up in some cinemas showing it.

subject: Wings of Desire
text: Its angels watch over a Berlin still divided by the Wall; two years later the Wall came down.

subject: Die Hard
text: The tower was the studio's real new office building, still under construction.

subject: Die Hard
text: The villain's shock as he falls is genuine: he was dropped a beat early.

subject: My Neighbor Totoro
text: It opened on a double bill with a film about two war orphans; some cinemas showed it second so children would leave happy.

subject: Do the Right Thing
text: Some critics predicted it would cause riots; it did not.

subject: When Harry Met Sally...
text: I'll have what she's having is spoken by the director's mother.

subject: The Silence of the Lambs
text: The doctor is on screen for only about sixteen minutes.

subject: Terminator 2: Judgment Day
text: About five minutes of liquid-metal effects took most of a year of computer work.

subject: Reservoir Dogs
text: It was shot in 30 days in an old mortuary; the ear-cutting scene made audience members walk out at nearly every festival screening.

subject: Jurassic Park
text: The dinosaurs were going to be stop-motion until a test of a computer-animated tyrannosaur changed everyone's mind.

subject: Jurassic Park
text: The raptors' hissing is the sound of tortoises mating.

subject: Schindler's List
text: Its director took no salary, calling it blood money.

subject: Groundhog Day
text: Estimates of how long the hero is stuck in the same day range from ten years to ten thousand. Its director said about ten.

subject: Pulp Fiction
text: The briefcase's contents were never decided; the glow is a light bulb.

subject: The Shawshank Redemption
text: A flop in cinemas, it became one of the most rented videos of all time and later topped popular polls.

subject: Forrest Gump
text: Its novelist was owed a share of the profits and was told the hit had made none; he settled after a public fight.

subject: Toy Story 2
text: A stray command deleted most of its files during production; a backup on a technical director's home computer, kept so she could work from home with a new baby, saved it.

subject: Heat
text: Its two great stars share only two scenes: a diner, and the end.

subject: Fargo
text: It opens by claiming to be a true story. It isn't.

subject: Titanic
text: The ship was built at nearly full size in a Mexican tank; the studio's then-record budget had the press predicting disaster.

subject: Titanic
text: The cast and crew were served chowder spiked with a hallucinogen on the last night in Nova Scotia; the culprit was never found.

subject: The Matrix
text: The green code is made of scanned Japanese sushi recipes.

subject: The Blair Witch Project
text: Its actors were given directions by notes hidden in milk crates and were kept hungry and frightened for real.

subject: Fight Club
text: Its marketing was so confused that the studio executive responsible was said to have lost his job over it.

subject: Spirited Away
text: Its bathhouse was inspired by its director's memories of a hot-spring inn and a museum of old buildings in Tokyo.

subject: The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring
text: All three parts were shot back to back over more than a year and a quarter in New Zealand.

subject: Amélie
text: The streets of Montmartre were digitally cleaned of graffiti and litter, which annoyed some French critics.

subject: City of God
text: Most of its actors were teenagers from the real favelas, cast through months of workshops.

subject: Oldboy
text: The hallway hammer fight is one unbroken take, rehearsed for days and shot over three.

subject: Brokeback Mountain
text: Its two leads were in their mid-twenties when it was shot; one of them died two years after it opened.

subject: No Country for Old Men
text: Its hitman's haircut was based on a 1979 photograph of a brothel customer.

subject: The Dark Knight
text: The truck flip in the street was done for real, in Chicago.

subject: The Dark Knight
text: The clown's clapping during the jail scene was improvised; the director kept it.

subject: Avatar
text: It ran so long in development that its director waited a decade for the technology he wanted.

subject: Inception
text: The rotating hallway was a real rotating set, built inside an airship hangar.

subject: The Social Network
text: The rowing twins were played by one actor, with another actor's body and a digital face.

subject: Mad Max: Fury Road
text: It was shot in the Namibian desert after rains made the Australian one bloom with flowers.

subject: Mad Max: Fury Road
text: Its director had no full script, only some 3,500 storyboard panels.

subject: La La Land
text: The wrong film was announced as Best Picture at the ceremony; its producers had already begun speeches.

subject: Parasite
text: The rich family's house was a set built on a studio lot, designed around where the sunlight would fall.

subject: Oppenheimer
text: The atomic test was done with real explosives and gasoline, no computer effects.

subject: Barbie
text: It caused a worldwide shortage of a particular shade of pink paint.

subject: Alfred Hitchcock
text: Appears in cameo in most of his own films; in a film set in a lifeboat he appears in a newspaper ad for a diet.

subject: Alfred Hitchcock
text: Said to have called actors cattle. He claimed he only said they should be treated like cattle.

subject: Charlie Chaplin
text: Once entered a lookalike contest of himself and did not win.

subject: Buster Keaton
text: Broke his neck doing a stunt with a water tower and didn't find out for years.

subject: Orson Welles
text: His radio broadcast of an alien invasion supposedly panicked America; he was given a studio contract on the strength of it.

subject: Akira Kurosawa
text: Nicknamed the Emperor for his perfectionism; he is said to have had a house roof removed because it spoiled a shot.

subject: Stanley Kubrick
text: Made actors do dozens, sometimes over a hundred, takes of a single shot.

subject: Steven Spielberg
text: Rejected by his film school of choice more than once; he later got an honorary degree from it.

subject: Federico Fellini
text: Kept a dream diary all his life and drew pictures of his dreams in it, many of which ended up on screen.

subject: Ingmar Bergman
text: Lived and worked on a small island in the Baltic for decades.

subject: Werner Herzog
text: Promised to eat his shoe if a student finished a documentary; he did, on camera, after boiling it with garlic.

subject: Werner Herzog
text: Said to have threatened his leading man with a rifle during a jungle shoot. Both men told the story, differently.

subject: Klaus Kinski
text: Said to have been so dreadful on one jungle shoot that a local chief offered to kill him for the director.

subject: Marilyn Monroe
text: Took her stage surname from her mother's family.

subject: James Dean
text: Made only three films as a lead; two were released after he died.

subject: Marlon Brando
text: Sent an activist to decline his second Oswald on his behalf, in protest at the film industry's treatment of Native Americans.

subject: Katharine Hepburn
text: Won four Oswalds for acting, a record, and attended the ceremony to collect none of them.

subject: John Wayne
text: Born Marion; the name was considered too soft by the studio.

subject: Bruce Lee
text: Was a cha-cha champion in Hong Kong before he was a martial-arts star.

subject: Jackie Chan
text: No insurance company will cover his stunts.

subject: Satyajit Ray
text: Designed his own posters and typefaces; one of his fonts is still in use.

subject: Amitabh Bachchan
text: Was rejected by a radio station because his voice was too deep; it became the most famous voice in India.

subject: Shah Rukh Khan
text: His house in Bombay draws crowds every birthday who gather outside to wave at him.

subject: Hayao Miyazaki
text: Announced his retirement several times and came back each time.

subject: Andrei Tarkovsky
text: Kept diaries he called Martyrolog, recording his battles with the authorities.

subject: Jean-Luc Godard
text: Said that all you need for a movie is a gun and a girl.

subject: Agnès Varda
text: Went to work as a still photographer at a theatre festival before ever having seen many films.
